articles.title: What are the main events for today?
articles.description: EUROPEAN SESSION In the European session, we don't have much on the agenda other than a couple of low-tier releases like the French PPI and ECB meeting minutes. The data won't change anything for the ECB, so the market reaction will be muted. As a reminder, the ECB is widely expected to hike interest rates by 25 bps in September, bringing the policy rate to 2.50%. This was also confirmed by "ECB sources" which reported that the central bank is ready to raise interest rates in September but added that there's little appetite to signal further tightening afterwards. AMERICAN SESSION In the American session, the only highlight is the US Jobless Claims figures. Initial Claims are expected at 208K vs 206K prior, while Continuing Claims are seen at 1790K vs 1799K prior. The US labour market has stabilised in recent weeks after a string of strong jobs data. Anyway, unless there are big deviations from expectations, the data is unlikely to be market-moving given the Fed's focus on inflation. CENTRAL BANK SPEAKERS 14:00 GMT/10:00 ET - Fed's Hammack (hawk - voter) This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

articles.title: The Guardian view on child marriage: girls should not be wives | Editorial
articles.description: There’s growing agreement that under-18s need to be protected – but international turmoil is pushing many towards wedlock Every minute, 23 girls around the world wed, according to the Girls Not Brides campaign, a coalition of more than 1,000 organisations across 100 countries. No child should be married. But girls are far more likely to be affected than boys, accounting for nine in 10 of those wed before 18, and their spouses are often much older men. The consequences, beyond the immediate threat of sexual violence, include the shortening of their education, increased risks of poverty and domestic abuse, and poor health, including high rates of maternal mortality. In spring, the Center for Global Development thinktank estimated that child marriage costs $175bn annually in lost productivity and increased health risks. The good news is that the last decade has seen a drop in rates; last year alone, Grenada, Bolivia, Burkina Faso, Kuwait and Portugal introduced bans. But there are disturbing signs of regression elsewhere. In May, the Taliban issued a new judicial code enabling child marriage below the previous minimum age of 16, and preventing wives from ending marriages they entered as children if their husbands object. Previous protections were inadequate and often poorly enforced; now even those have been swept away. Activists say forced and early marriages have soared since the Taliban returned to power in 2021, thanks to the ban on secondary education and the state of the economy. Continue reading...
